title: The Opposition Begins
subtitle: Tribal Resistance, Diplomatic Pressure, and Resolute Faith
summary: The economic and tribal reasons for Quraysh's resistance, delegations of chieftains to Abu Talib, the Prophet's immortal words of steadfastness, attempts at bribery and negotiation, and the smear campaigns launched by Makkan aristocrats.

sections.text: The Motivations Behind Makkan Resistance

Following the open proclamation of Islam, the chieftains of Quraysh realized that the new faith was not merely a personal philosophical reflection, but a direct challenge to the social, economic, and religious order of Makkah. For generations, Quraysh had enjoyed unrivalled prestige across Arabia as custodians of the Kaaba and its three hundred and sixty tribal deities. Pilgrims from every province brought wealth, offered sacrifices, and patronized Makkan markets.

To proclaim that these carved idols were lifeless stones incapable of benefit or harm was, in the eyes of the oligarchs, to undermine the pilgrimage economy and invite tribal rebellion. Moreover, the Islamic message of universal human equality directly threatened the aristocratic hierarchy led by men such as Abu Jahl ('Amr ibn Hisham), Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.
The bustling commercial squares of Makkah where clan chieftains plotted against the new message.
Tribal Delegations to Abu Talib

In Arabian society, a person's safety depended on the protection of his clan (jiwar). As head of Banu Hashim, Abu Talib protected his nephew from physical harm, though he did not himself accept Islam. Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim report that at his death he declared that he remained on the religion of 'Abd al-Muttalib; this is the predominant position among Sunni scholars, while some later scholars, especially in Shi'i scholarship, hold that he was a believer. Frustrated by his protection, the chiefs of Quraysh sent delegations to him.

Ibn Ishaq relates that in their first delegation they said to him: 'O Abu Talib! Your nephew has insulted our gods, denounced our religion, called our way of life foolish, and declared our forefathers misguided. Either restrain him, or leave us to deal with him, for you are of our religion in opposing him.' Abu Talib answered them gently, and they went away.

When the Prophet continued his preaching unabated, a second, sterner delegation arrived, issuing an explicit ultimatum: 'O Abu Talib! You possess seniority, nobility, and status among us. We asked you to restrain your nephew and you did not. By Allah, we cannot endure having our fathers insulted and our gods mocked! Either restrain him, or we will fight both you and him until one of the two parties perishes!'
The Sun in the Right Hand and Moon in the Left

Ibn Ishaq relates that the threat weighed heavily on Abu Talib, who did not wish to break with his people or to abandon his nephew. He sent for Muhammad, told him what Quraysh had said, and asked him: 'Spare me and spare yourself, and do not burden me with more than I can bear.'

In Ibn Ishaq's account, the Prophet thought that his uncle might be about to abandon him, and he answered with the words for which this episode is remembered. Ibn Ishaq transmits it through Ya'qub ibn 'Utbah without a complete chain, and hadith critics regard it as weak, though the episode is very widely related in the sirah literature:

"O my uncle! By God, if they were to place the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left on condition that I abandon this matter, until God makes it prevail or I perish in it, I would not abandon it." — Ibn Ishaq, in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham (a report with an incomplete chain)

Then, Ibn Ishaq continues, the Prophet's eyes filled with tears and he rose to leave. Abu Talib called him back and said: 'Go, my nephew, and say what you wish. By God, I will never hand you over for anything.'
Attempts at Bribery and Diplomatic Compromise

Failing to move Abu Talib, Quraysh turned to offers of worldly reward. Ibn Ishaq relates, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi without a connected chain, that they sent 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, an eloquent chief of Banu 'Abd Shams, to speak with Muhammad while he sat alone in the sanctuary.

'Utbah sat before Muhammad and said: 'O son of my brother, you have brought a momentous matter to your people. If you desire wealth by this cause, we will gather from our riches until you are the wealthiest among us. If you seek status and honor, we will make you our sovereign king so that no decision is made without you. And if this vision is an illness that visits you, we will expend our wealth on physicians until you are cured.'

Muhammad listened patiently without interrupting. When 'Utbah concluded, the Prophet asked gently: 'Have you finished, O Abu al-Walid?' He answered: 'Yes.' The Prophet said: 'Then listen to me.' He began reciting the majestic opening verses of Surah Fussilat: 'Ha Meem. A revelation from the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful — A Book whose verses have been detailed, an Arabic Quran for a people who know...'

In Ibn Ishaq's account, 'Utbah listened, leaning back on his hands, until the Prophet reached the verse of prostration and prostrated; then the Prophet said: 'You have heard what you have heard, O Abu al-Walid; it is up to you.' 'Utbah returned to Quraysh and advised them: 'Leave this man to what he is doing. By God, I have heard words the like of which I have never heard.' They replied that Muhammad had bewitched him with his tongue, and rejected his advice. Other narrations of the episode, in later collections, say that 'Utbah stopped the Prophet at an earlier verse of the surah.
The quiet rocky paths of Makkah where the early believers persevered amidst rising hostility.
Smear Campaigns and Ideological Warfare

Ibn Ishaq relates that as the pilgrimage season approached, Quraysh gathered around al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah to agree on what they would tell visiting Arabs about Muhammad. They proposed calling him a kahin (soothsayer), a majnun (madman) or a sha'ir (poet), but al-Walid rejected each, saying that none of these descriptions fitted what they had heard.

Eventually, they settled on labeling him a sahir (sorcerer) who possessed speech that separated man from his father, brother, wife, and clan. Stationing agents at every mountain entrance into Makkah during the pilgrimage season, they warned travelers against listening to Muhammad. Yet this very campaign inadvertently spread his name to every corner of Arabia, preparing distant tribes for the eventual embrace of Islam.
